title: Computer Science
purpose: Define the governed use of computational models, abstractions, theories, and methods to understand, design, analyze, and verify systems without confusing a mathematical result with an implemented or acceptable system.
why_it_matters: Computer science provides the abstractions used to reason about computation, information, algorithms, languages, systems, and limits. Unstated assumptions can make a formally valid result irrelevant to real users, data, resources, security, or lifecycle conditions.
applies_when: Applies when computational complexity, correctness, formal models, algorithms, data structures, languages, concurrency, distributed behavior, information representation, or theoretical limits affect a design or decision.
does_not_apply_when: Not applicable to a purely descriptive or bounded editorial change with no computational claim, model, method, requirement, implementation, or evidence consequence. Record the exact scope and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires an authorized question, domain and requirements context, declared assumptions, relevant data or formal definitions, qualified review, and a reproducible method. Related architecture, security, privacy, safety, and performance constraints must be available or marked unresolved.
required_inputs: Question, definitions, inputs, constraints, model, proof or experiment method, expected properties, complexity target, resource limits, threat assumptions, evidence standard, and acceptance authority.
human_authority: Humans set the question, acceptable abstraction, values, constraints, interpretation, risk, and acceptance. They approve claims that affect architecture, policy, safety, rights, or investment and ensure qualified independent review.
ai_boundary: AI may explain concepts, propose models, derive examples, check reasoning, generate experiments, and identify counterexamples. It must label conjecture, proof, simulation, and empirical result separately; it must not invent a proof, hide assumptions, or approve consequential conclusions.
evidence_requirements: Evidence identifies definitions, model version, inputs, method, environment, seed or nondeterminism, resource limits, reviewer, result, and excluded claims. Missing or inconclusive evidence is not success.
failure_anti_patterns: Unstated assumptions, asymptotic claims treated as production performance, simulation treated as proof, proof treated as user acceptance, ignored resource limits, and AI-generated reasoning accepted without checking.
recovery: Preserve the prior claim and evidence when a counterexample, assumption change, or reproducibility failure appears. Narrow use, rerun analysis, obtain qualified review, or supersede through an attributable decision; do not erase the failed result.
completion: The question, model, assumptions, method, result, limits, review, acceptance authority, and engineering implications are explicit, reproducible within declared conditions, and free of unrecorded material gaps.
source_gaps: Based on the Canonical Section Contract and shared governance conventions. The Codex does not select a universal formalism, proof assistant, computational model, curriculum, or domain-specific acceptance threshold; those remain system-specific gaps.

title: Algorithm Engineering
purpose: Define the selection, design, implementation, analysis, testing, tuning, deployment, monitoring, and retirement of algorithms that transform inputs into outputs or decisions under explicit correctness, complexity, resource, security, fairness, safety, and human-control constraints.
why_it_matters: Algorithmic errors can be systematic, invisible, amplified by scale, or mistaken for neutral automation. Engineering must expose tradeoffs, edge cases, distribution changes, adversarial inputs, and the difference between technical output and authorized decision.
applies_when: Applies to deterministic, randomized, heuristic, optimization, search, ranking, scheduling, control, cryptographic, statistical, or learned algorithms with material system effects.
does_not_apply_when: A trivial explanatory example or bounded refactoring with no algorithmic behavior, contract, performance, data, risk, or evidence effect may be exempt. Record the algorithm baseline and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires requirements, objective function, input and output contracts, data characteristics, constraints, threat model, resource budget, quality measures, and acceptance authority. Domain, privacy, security, safety, and accessibility obligations must be identified.
required_inputs: Problem definition, inputs, outputs, invariants, objective, constraints, complexity target, workload, data, error tolerance, adversary model, baseline, alternatives, test oracle, evidence method, and lifecycle conditions.
human_authority: Humans approve the objective, tradeoffs, protected constraints, acceptable error, risk, deployment, and use of outputs in consequential decisions. They ensure affected parties and qualified reviewers are represented.
ai_boundary: AI may propose algorithms, explain tradeoffs, generate reference implementations and tests, find counterexamples, and analyze traces. It must expose assumptions and uncertainty, not fabricate complexity or benchmark results, and must not select or deploy a consequential algorithm without authority.
evidence_requirements: Record data, workload, environment, configuration, seed, metrics, uncertainty, baselines, excluded populations, reviewer, and limitations. Benchmark results do not prove field performance or acceptable outcomes.
failure_anti_patterns: Optimizing a proxy while harming the outcome, ignoring worst-case behavior, leaking sensitive inputs, treating ranking as neutral, using stale benchmarks, hiding error distributions, and deploying without drift or fallback controls.
recovery: On defect, drift, unsafe output, resource exhaustion, or evidence loss, stop or narrow use, preserve inputs and outputs, notify the owner, use an approved prior version or manual path, and record compensation for external effects. Reopen when objective, data, constraints, or population changes.
completion: The algorithm and its use are bounded, specified, implemented, independently tested, evidenced, accepted for the exact scope, monitored, and supported by a truthful recovery and retirement plan.
source_gaps: Based on the Canonical Section Contract and shared governance conventions. Domain-specific fairness, safety, statistical, cryptographic, and regulatory thresholds remain unresolved until the system owner supplies them.

title: Programming Language Engineering
purpose: Define the governed design, implementation, evolution, tooling, verification, distribution, and retirement of programming languages and their ecosystems, including syntax, semantics, type systems, compilers, runtimes, libraries, diagnostics, compatibility, and migration.
why_it_matters: Language behavior is infrastructure for every program written in it. Ambiguous semantics, unsound typing, compiler divergence, runtime incompatibility, or poor diagnostics can create failures far beyond the language project.
applies_when: Applies when a language, dialect, DSL, compiler, interpreter, virtual machine, standard library, formatter, linter, debugger, package ecosystem, or compatibility guarantee is designed or changed.
does_not_apply_when: A project merely using an established language without changing its language, toolchain, compatibility, or conformance claims is not itself language engineering. Record the consumed baseline and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires language goals, semantic model, grammar, type and memory model, runtime assumptions, target platforms, threat model, compatibility horizon, conformance suite, licensing, and human acceptance authority.
required_inputs: Use cases, syntax, semantics, grammar, type rules, evaluation order, error model, resource and safety limits, ABI or interface rules, implementation strategy, tests, benchmarks, compatibility and migration requirements.
human_authority: Humans approve semantics, safety and security tradeoffs, compatibility breaks, ecosystem commitments, licensing, release, deprecation, and retirement. Qualified language and systems reviewers must challenge material claims.
ai_boundary: AI may draft grammar, examples, tests, documentation, diagnostics, and implementation proposals. It must not invent semantic authority, declare conformance, hide incompatibility, or release a compiler or runtime without delegated review and evidence.
evidence_requirements: Evidence identifies specification version, implementation, target, test corpus, environment, result, deviations, reviewer, and limitations. Passing examples do not prove complete conformance, safety, or ecosystem compatibility.
failure_anti_patterns: Undocumented semantics, compiler-specific behavior presented as standard, unsound optimization, silent breaking change, unsafe runtime default, incomplete diagnostics, unbounded resource use, and a migration plan that depends on the retired toolchain.
recovery: Quarantine the affected release, preserve source and artifacts, route users to a supported version or compatibility mode, publish the defect and impact, and use compensation for external effects. Reopen the specification when evidence or intended semantics change.
completion: Semantics, implementation, conformance, compatibility, security, support, migration, evidence, ownership, and retirement are explicit for the declared version and targets.

title: Compiler Engineering
purpose: Define the governed construction and evolution of compilers, interpreters, linkers, optimizers, assemblers, and associated tooling that translate source programs into executable or intermediate forms.
why_it_matters: Translation defects can change program meaning, weaken security, corrupt data, or create platform-specific failures. Compiler success is not proof that the source intent or target behavior is correct.
applies_when: Applies to compiler, interpreter, assembler, linker, optimizer, code generator, transpiler, static analyzer, debugger, build backend, or language-toolchain change.
does_not_apply_when: Using an unchanged, supported toolchain without changing its behavior or trust boundary is not compiler engineering. Record the consumed version and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires language specification, source and target model, ABI, optimization constraints, threat model, supported platforms, build inputs, conformance tests, licensing, and release authority.
required_inputs: Grammar and semantics, intermediate representation, passes, diagnostics, target architecture, runtime and ABI, optimization invariants, reproducibility needs, test corpus, performance and security limits.
human_authority: Humans approve semantics, optimization risk, target support, security posture, compatibility breaks, release, and retirement; independent qualified review is required for safety or security-sensitive claims.
ai_boundary: AI may draft passes, tests, diagnostics, documentation, and code review findings. It must not invent language semantics, claim conformance, hide miscompilation, or publish artifacts without human authorization and evidence.
evidence_requirements: Identify source, compiler, target, flags, dependencies, environment, corpus, expected and actual output, reviewer, deviations, and limits. Benchmarks and successful compilation do not prove semantic correctness.
failure_anti_patterns: Unreviewed optimization, target-specific miscompilation, unsigned binaries, hidden build flags, stale test corpus, unsafe diagnostics, silent ABI break, and treating compiler speed as program correctness.
recovery: Quarantine affected versions, preserve source and binaries, notify users, provide a supported prior toolchain or compensation path, and publish impact. Reopen the specification when semantics, targets, or evidence change.
completion: The declared toolchain is specified, reproducible, tested, reviewed, evidenced, supported, and accepted for exact targets and versions with compatibility and retirement plans.

title: Runtime Engineering
purpose: Define the design, implementation, verification, operation, and retirement of execution environments that load, schedule, isolate, monitor, and support software.
why_it_matters: Runtime behavior determines what software actually does under load, failure, concurrency, and hostile input. A healthy process or passing unit test cannot establish runtime safety or correctness.
applies_when: Applies to virtual machines, interpreters, managed runtimes, containers, schedulers, garbage collectors, loaders, plugin hosts, sandboxes, and execution libraries.
does_not_apply_when: An application consuming an unchanged supported runtime is not runtime engineering; record the runtime baseline and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires language and functional contracts, resource and isolation model, target environment, threat model, workload, compatibility, observability, recovery, and acceptance authority.
required_inputs: Execution semantics, memory and concurrency model, scheduling, quotas, isolation, startup and shutdown, errors, signals, telemetry, upgrade, platform constraints, tests, and support horizon.
human_authority: Humans approve isolation, resource, safety, privacy, security, compatibility, release, incident, and retirement decisions. Operators retain stop and recovery authority.
ai_boundary: AI may analyze traces, draft runtime code or tests, and propose tuning. It must not change production scheduling, quotas, isolation, or recovery without delegation and evidence; model advice remains advisory.
evidence_requirements: Identify workload, host, runtime, configuration, resource limits, inputs, environment, method, output, reviewer, and limitations. Health metrics do not prove correct or safe execution.
failure_anti_patterns: Unbounded resource use, shared mutable state without control, hidden host dependence, silent data loss on shutdown, missing telemetry, unsafe plugin loading, and tuning that sacrifices isolation or recovery.
recovery: Stop or isolate the affected runtime, preserve state and evidence, use an approved fallback or prior version, restore or compensate external effects, and reopen after root-cause and evidence review.
completion: Execution semantics, resources, isolation, observability, recovery, compatibility, ownership, evidence, and operational support are explicit and verified for declared hosts and workloads.

title: Operating Systems Engineering
purpose: Define the engineering of operating-system services that manage hardware, processes, memory, files, devices, identity, isolation, scheduling, and system calls.
why_it_matters: Operating systems mediate nearly every resource and authority. A defect can compromise confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, or recoverability across all applications.
applies_when: Applies to kernels, system services, distributions, boot systems, filesystems, process models, security subsystems, device support, and OS-level configuration or update.
does_not_apply_when: Using an unchanged supported OS without altering OS behavior, configuration baseline, trust boundary, or support claim is not OS engineering; record the baseline.
prerequisites: Requires hardware and platform model, threat model, privilege model, resource goals, compatibility, update, backup, recovery, testing, support, and acceptance authority.
required_inputs: System calls, processes, memory, storage, scheduling, identity, permissions, boot, update, logging, hardware, drivers, failure, recovery, target platforms, and lifecycle obligations.
human_authority: Humans approve privilege, security, safety, compatibility, update, release, incident, and retirement decisions. They retain authority to isolate, stop, restore, and accept residual risk.
ai_boundary: AI may analyze source and telemetry, draft tests and documentation, and propose fixes. It must not alter kernel, privilege, boot, update, or recovery controls without explicit authority and independent review.
evidence_requirements: Identify hardware, OS, configuration, privilege, test, environment, result, reviewer, and limitations. A booted host or patch result does not prove secure or reliable operation.
failure_anti_patterns: Running as administrator, unsigned updates, shared secrets, hidden driver assumptions, missing recovery media, suppressed kernel errors, unbounded resource use, and destructive rollback that erases evidence.
recovery: Isolate affected hosts, preserve forensic and operational evidence, use safe boot or approved prior image, restore or replace hardware, compensate external effects, and reopen after independent review.
completion: The OS behavior, privilege, platform, security, update, compatibility, recovery, evidence, ownership, support, and retirement boundaries are explicit and verified.

title: Kernel Engineering
purpose: Define the design, implementation, verification, operation, and retirement of a kernel and its privileged mechanisms for scheduling, memory, interrupts, devices, isolation, and system calls.
why_it_matters: Kernel defects have system-wide blast radius and can defeat higher-level controls. Privileged code requires stronger evidence, isolation, review, and recovery than ordinary application code.
applies_when: Applies to kernel code, hypervisor-like privileged layers, schedulers, memory managers, interrupt paths, system-call interfaces, and kernel configuration or extensions.
does_not_apply_when: A project using an unchanged supported kernel without modifying its privileged behavior or trust boundary is not kernel engineering; record the baseline and trigger.
prerequisites: Requires hardware model, privilege and threat model, invariants, ABI, performance and safety goals, source and build provenance, fault model, test environment, update, recovery, and acceptance authority.
required_inputs: Scheduling, memory, interrupts, concurrency, system calls, isolation, devices, boot, fault handling, observability, resource budgets, security properties, tests, and lifecycle constraints.
human_authority: Humans approve privileged behavior, security and safety tradeoffs, release, patch, emergency response, and retirement. Independent review and explicit residual-risk acceptance are required.
ai_boundary: AI may inspect code, draft tests, identify races, and propose changes. It must not modify or release privileged code, claim absence of vulnerabilities, or suppress findings without delegated authority and independent verification.
evidence_requirements: Identify hardware, kernel, configuration, test, fault injection, environment, result, reviewer, and limitations. Passing boot or benchmark evidence does not prove privileged safety.
failure_anti_patterns: Unreviewed privileged code, hidden race conditions, missing symbols, unsafe module loading, disabled security controls, untested recovery, and erasing crash or audit evidence during rollback.
recovery: Stop or isolate affected systems, preserve crash and audit evidence, use safe boot or trusted prior image, restore or replace hardware, compensate external effects, and reopen after root-cause review.
completion: The kernel contract, privilege boundaries, invariants, implementation, evidence, compatibility, update, recovery, support, and retirement are explicit and independently reviewed.

title: Driver Engineering
purpose: Define the design, implementation, verification, deployment, operation, update, and retirement of software that controls or exposes hardware devices within explicit safety, security, performance, compatibility, and recovery boundaries.
why_it_matters: Drivers cross the hardware and privileged software boundary. A fault can corrupt data, bypass isolation, damage equipment, or make recovery unavailable.
applies_when: Applies to kernel, user-space, firmware-adjacent, virtual, bus, device, sensor, actuator, and compatibility drivers.
does_not_apply_when: Using an unchanged supported driver without altering behavior, configuration, trust boundary, or support claim is not driver engineering; record the baseline.
prerequisites: Requires hardware specification, protocol, timing, privilege, threat, safety, lifecycle, test equipment, platform, update, and recovery requirements.
required_inputs: Device behavior, discovery, initialization, I/O, concurrency, errors, timeouts, power, permissions, data integrity, diagnostics, compatibility, and failure model.
human_authority: Humans approve hardware access, privilege, safety, release, field update, residual risk, and retirement. Operators retain isolation and recovery authority.

recovery: Isolate device, preserve logs and state, enter approved safe state, use prior driver or manual control, replace hardware if needed, compensate effects, and reopen after independent review.
completion: Hardware and driver contracts, permissions, safety, compatibility, evidence, support, update, recovery, and retirement are explicit for declared devices and platforms.

title: Middleware Engineering

does_not_apply_when: An application using an unchanged approved middleware component is not middleware engineering; record the consumed baseline and reopening trigger.

required_inputs: Interfaces, schemas, identity, ordering, delivery, retries, idempotency, transactions, timeouts, backpressure, quotas, telemetry, upgrades, and recovery.
human_authority: Humans approve shared defaults, security, compatibility, service commitments, risk, release, and deprecation. Consumer owners remain accountable for local consequences.

title: Full-Stack Engineering
purpose: Define coordinated engineering across user interface, client, service, integration, data, deployment, and operational boundaries for an end-to-end product or service.
why_it_matters: Cross-layer failures often hide at boundaries: stale state, mismatched contracts, unauthorized calls, inaccessible recovery, or data changes that no single team sees.

title: Web Engineering
purpose: Define engineering of web applications and services across browser, server, network, content, identity, accessibility, performance, security, and delivery boundaries.

title: Data Analysis
purpose: Define a governed method for turning authorized data into bounded descriptive, diagnostic, exploratory, and decision-support findings. Data Analysis preserves the difference between observation, calculation, interpretation, recommendation, and decision.
why_it_matters: Analysis can make incomplete or biased data appear authoritative. A clear analytical chain lets owners distinguish what the data shows from what an analyst infers and what a decision maker chooses.
applies_when: Applies when data is used to describe conditions, explain variation, compare groups, diagnose causes, monitor outcomes, support decisions, or assess a change. It applies more deeply when results affect rights, safety, finance, service, policy, models, or public claims.
does_not_apply_when: May be recorded as non-applicable for formatting, transcription, or reversible inspection with no analytical claim or material decision effect. The record must name scope, owner, evidence date, and reopening trigger; a chart or query is not automatically exempt.

human_authority: The human owner approves the question, population, sensitive uses, interpretation, decision threshold, publication, and acceptance. Humans resolve ambiguous meaning, competing interests, residual risk, and action; analysts must not turn findings into policy without authority.
ai_boundary: AI may profile, summarize, calculate, visualize, detect patterns, propose analyses, and identify gaps within authorized data. It must show provenance and uncertainty and must not invent observations, infer permission, hide adverse results, or present correlation as causation.
evidence_requirements: Each claim identifies source, version, population, period, method, transformation, analyst or tool, result, uncertainty, and limitation. Samples, dashboards, correlations, and model-generated summaries support only bounded claims. Missing or contradictory evidence is marked UNKNOWN or NOT VERIFIED.
failure_anti_patterns: Cherry-picked periods; p-hacking; silent filtering; denominator changes; proxy measures treated as outcomes; causal language from correlation; data leakage; hidden missingness; unauthorized disclosure; automated recommendations presented as decisions; and untraceable spreadsheet edits.
recovery: Quarantine affected outputs when lineage, quality, permission, or method fails. Preserve prior artifacts, identify safe uses, notify owners, correct or rerun from a governed source, and reassess decisions that relied on invalid findings. Reopen after population, definition, policy, or source change.
completion: The question, scope, source, method, transformations, results, uncertainty, limitations, controls, verification, owner decision, and reopening condition are recorded. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE until source reconciliation and owner acceptance are separately completed.

title: Statistics
purpose: Define governed statistical reasoning for describing uncertainty, estimating quantities, testing claims, designing samples and experiments, and supporting decisions without overstating precision or causality.
why_it_matters: Statistical language can conceal consequential assumptions. Confidence intervals, significance tests, forecasts, and averages are useful only when their population, design, uncertainty, and limits are understood.
applies_when: Applies to estimation, inference, forecasting, experimentation, sampling, measurement, risk quantification, quality control, and statistical claims. Greater review is required for regulated, rights-affecting, safety, financial, or public decisions.
does_not_apply_when: May be non-applicable to exact deterministic counts or formatting with no inferential, predictive, comparative, or decision claim. Record the bounded rationale and reopening trigger; a small sample is not a reason to omit statistical qualification.
prerequisites: Requires a defined population, data lineage, measurement meaning, sampling frame, domain context, and decision owner. Depends on Sections 154, 156, 163, 164, 180, and 254 for modeling, quality, analysis, evaluation, and tests.
required_inputs: Estimand; population; sampling frame; unit; design; outcome; covariates; missing-data plan; assumptions; model; prior or baseline; error tolerance; power or precision target; multiplicity; subgroup plan; and decision consequences.
human_authority: Humans approve estimands, assumptions, acceptable error, subgroup treatment, stopping rules, publication, and use. A qualified statistician may advise, but only the owner accepts residual uncertainty and resulting action.
ai_boundary: AI may calculate, simulate, explain, compare methods, and flag violations. It must expose assumptions and code or procedure, preserve exact inputs, and must not invent p-values, confidence, samples, causal effects, or significance.
evidence_requirements: Each result identifies population, sample, design, period, measure, method, assumptions, software or tool version, uncertainty, reviewer, and limitation. Significance, precision, and forecast accuracy support only bounded claims and never prove causation alone.
failure_anti_patterns: P-hacking; optional stopping; multiple testing without control; Simpson's paradox ignored; ecological fallacy; confidence mistaken for probability of truth; averages hiding harm; causal claims from association; and fabricated statistical certainty.
recovery: Quarantine results when assumptions, data, sampling, or calculations fail. Preserve prior outputs, identify affected decisions, rerun or revise with qualified review, and notify owners. Reopen after population, measure, policy, data, or decision changes.
completion: Estimand, design, data, method, assumptions, results, uncertainty, limitations, verification, and owner decision are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE until source reconciliation and owner acceptance.

why_it_matters: Optimization can produce an efficient answer to the wrong objective or consume hidden safety, equity, accessibility, or resilience margins. Operations Research makes objectives and constraints inspectable before a solver's output becomes action.

human_authority: Humans set objectives, protected constraints, tradeoffs, priorities, exceptions, and acceptance. They decide whether to act, communicate, or override a recommendation. Analysts cannot relax a constraint or commit resources without explicit authority.
ai_boundary: AI may formulate alternatives, solve bounded problems, simulate scenarios, and explain sensitivity. It must expose objective and constraint choices and cannot hide infeasibility, manipulate weights, claim optimality without proof, or execute without delegation.

title: AI Safety
purpose: Define the identification, prevention, evaluation, monitoring, containment, and recovery of AI harms, including unsafe capability, misuse, failure, loss of control, human impact, and system interaction risk.
why_it_matters: AI failures can scale, persist, deceive, discriminate, or interact with tools and institutions. Safety is a system property requiring human authority and recovery, not a model score or warning label.
applies_when: Applies to any AI system with material user, public, physical, environmental, financial, privacy, security, rights, or autonomy consequence. Depth is proportional to hazard and reversibility.
does_not_apply_when: May be non-applicable to bounded non-AI work or analysis with no AI claim or consequence. Record exact scope and reopen if capability, use, population, or integration changes.
prerequisites: Requires system boundary, hazard analysis, domain and user evidence, threat model, evaluation, operating concept, incident authority, and owner acceptance. Depends on Sections 050, 167-170, 180, 181, 183-185, and 188.
required_inputs: Use; hazards; affected parties; model and system; tools; data; autonomy; operating environment; constraints; safety requirements; tests; monitoring; stop and fallback; communications; and compensation authority.
human_authority: Humans own safety decisions, hazard acceptance, release, emergency action, notification, and retirement. Independent safety specialists may block unsafe work. AI cannot self-certify safety or waive a hazard.
ai_boundary: AI may identify hazards, generate scenarios, simulate failures, and monitor bounded signals. It must expose uncertainty and escalate. It must not suppress safety findings, redefine hazards, or continue after revoked authority.
evidence_requirements: Each safety claim identifies hazard, scope, system version, scenario, control, test, result, uncertainty, reviewer, date, and limitation. A test suite, refusal rate, or compliance statement is not universal safety evidence.
failure_anti_patterns: Safety as documentation only; hazard omission; model-only boundary; no independent stop; warning as control; risk accepted by default; hidden near misses; and recovery dependent on the failed AI system.
recovery: Contain and stop affected behavior on a credible hazard or control failure. Preserve immutable decisions and evidence, protect affected parties, communicate, compensate where authorized, investigate independently, and require fresh safety review before resuming.
completion: Hazards, controls, tests, evidence, residual risk, authority, stop, recovery, communication, and reopening are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending reconciliation and owner acceptance.

title: AI Governance
purpose: Define the authority, policy, accountability, evidence, approval, monitoring, and lifecycle controls for AI systems and AI-enabled mutations.
why_it_matters: Governance fails when a local check is mistaken for policy evaluation, a model capability becomes authority, or an approval cannot be replayed. Explicit records make decisions accountable, reviewable, and reversible only through compensation.
applies_when: Applies to AI design, procurement, training, evaluation, deployment, operation, tool use, data use, prompt changes, policy changes, and retirement. It applies more deeply with regulated use, autonomy, sensitive data, external effect, or mutation.
does_not_apply_when: May be non-applicable to non-AI work or read-only analysis with no AI claim, policy effect, or mutation. Record scope, controlling policy, owner, evidence date, and reopening trigger.
prerequisites: Requires authority model, policy sources, impact assessment, AI inventory, data and system context, evaluation, safety, privacy, security, and audit capability. Depends on Sections 048, 056, 180, 182, 184, 185, and 188.
required_inputs: Intent; actor; AI system; purpose; data; model; provider; capability; resource; mutation class; traceId; capability token; GovernanceContext; PolicyEvaluationRequest and Result; quorum; resolution policy; and compensation path.
human_authority: Humans define policy, delegate authority, approve exceptions, provide quorum where required, accept risk, review evidence, and authorize or deny mutations. No operator override may erase a prior immutable decision or bypass policy evaluation.
ai_boundary: AI may prepare requests, summarize policy, identify gaps, and recommend decisions. It must not treat local validation as governance evaluation, self-issue capability, approve itself, or mutate without a complete binding and valid decision.
evidence_requirements: Every governance claim identifies policy, evaluation ID and result, traceId, actor, capability scope, resource, action, mutation class, decision, quorum, evidence, and validity. Local tests, approvals, or logs alone do not prove governed authorization.
failure_anti_patterns: Rubber-stamp approval; policy copied into prompt; local-only enforcement; self-approval; incomplete binding; hidden override; mutable decision; audit replacement; quorum bypass; and destructive reversal.
recovery: Deny or stop on binding, evaluation, capability, quorum, trace, or policy failure. Preserve records, identify safe read-only work, obtain fresh evaluation and approval, and use compensation transactions linked to prior decisions rather than destructive reversal.
completion: Authority, policy, evaluation, binding, decision, audit, trace, quorum, mutation, observability, compensation, and lifecycle are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending reconciliation and owner acceptance.

why_it_matters: Automation can accelerate an unapproved or invalid model into production. MLOps must preserve evidence and authority across frequent data, code, model, and infrastructure changes.

title: Synthetic Data Engineering
purpose: Define governed creation, validation, use, disclosure, retention, and retirement of data generated to resemble or simulate real data for development, testing, analysis, training, evaluation, or operations.
why_it_matters: Synthetic data can reduce exposure but can also memorize, reproduce, amplify bias, create unrealistic correlations, or be treated as real evidence. Its value and limits must be measured for the intended use.
applies_when: Applies to generated records, simulations, augmented samples, masked or perturbed data, test fixtures, synthetic images, text, audio, features, labels, and training or evaluation data. Depth increases with sensitive source data or consequential models.
does_not_apply_when: May be non-applicable to hand-written non-sensitive test constants with no claim of realism, privacy, or population representation. Record scope, owner, source status, and reopening trigger.

human_authority: Humans approve source use, privacy target, generator, disclosure, realism claim, downstream use, and retention. Data owners and privacy authorities decide whether synthetic output remains sensitive or linkable.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Operations

title: Cybersecurity Engineering
purpose: Establish and maintain engineered protections for confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, accountability, privacy, safety, and user control across the system lifecycle. Cybersecurity Engineering converts approved risk, threat, governance, architecture, and operational requirements into defensible controls and measurable residual risk.
why_it_matters: Security failures can harm people, expose records, corrupt decisions, interrupt essential services, and destroy evidence. Security is a system property requiring coordinated engineering, operation, governance, and human judgment rather than a scan result or product feature.
applies_when: Applies when systems, data, identities, devices, facilities, suppliers, interfaces, models, or operations face unauthorized access, misuse, disruption, manipulation, disclosure, or loss. It applies proportionally to consequence, exposure, and recovery dependence.
does_not_apply_when: May be recorded only when an approved current security architecture covers the exact scope, version, environment, data, threat conditions, and change with no material effect. Purely descriptive or synthetic work may remain proposed, but cannot claim security acceptance.
prerequisites: Sections 018, 019, 020, 021-048, and 050-052 provide risk, requirements, system, architecture, governance, safety, reliability, and resilience context. Owners for assets, threats, controls, exceptions, incidents, evidence, and acceptance must be named.
required_inputs: Asset inventory, data classifications, trust boundaries, users, operators, dependencies, threat intelligence, risk appetite, control objectives, policies, architecture, vulnerabilities, incidents, recovery targets, and legal or contractual obligations.
human_authority: The human authority defines protected outcomes, accepts residual risk, approves exceptions, assigns owners, authorizes testing, and decides containment, disclosure, recovery, and acceptance. Security engineers advise and implement within that authority.
ai_boundary: AI may inventory, correlate, model threats, draft controls, analyze telemetry, and propose tests. It must preserve provenance and uncertainty, cannot infer permission or approve risk, cannot expose secrets, and must escalate ambiguous authority, active harm, or incomplete evidence.
evidence_requirements: Claims identify asset, version, environment, threat, method, scope, time, evidence source, owner, result, uncertainty, and limitation. Scans, benchmarks, attestations, and clean tests prove only their bounded claim. Failed, stale, missing, or contradictory evidence constrains status.
failure_anti_patterns: Treating a scan, certificate, firewall, or green dashboard as total security; unowned assets; security by obscurity; unlogged privileged access; shared secrets; missing recovery; ignoring suppliers and humans; optimizing availability or convenience by weakening control; and allowing AI to suppress findings or act beyond authority.
recovery: Contain, isolate, preserve volatile and durable evidence, revoke affected authority, communicate through approved channels, and record the decision chain. Recover from known-good artifacts or approved compensation, validate downstream impact, reassess residual risk, and reopen when threat, scope, architecture, data, or evidence changes.
completion: Scope, assets, threats, owners, controls, evidence, testing, residual risk, exceptions, recovery, and acceptance are explicit. Normal and hostile paths are tested, unresolved gaps constrain status, and the result remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending source reconciliation, hostile review, and owner acceptance.

Supplied material does not define one universal risk standard, threat library, sector regime, control catalog, evidence retention period, or recovery target; these remain scope-specific gaps.

why_it_matters: Application defects are often reachable through ordinary user and integration paths. A build can succeed while injection, privilege escalation, data leakage, insecure defaults, or unsafe recovery remains exploitable.
applies_when: Applies to web, mobile, desktop, service, API, batch, event, agent, plugin, and administrative applications, including code, configuration, libraries, pipelines, and runtime interfaces.
does_not_apply_when: Only where an approved application security baseline covers exact artifact, version, configuration, environment, data, interface, and change with no material effect. Prototypes remain proposed and cannot claim secure implementation.
prerequisites: Sections 019, 030-032, 045-048, 107-129, 246, 260, 270, and 301-309 provide requirements, information, application, identity, security, engineering, testing, dependency, delivery, and operations context.
required_inputs: Source and build artifacts, dependency inventory, data flows, identities, roles, endpoints, threat model, coding standards, security requirements, configurations, test results, vulnerabilities, incidents, and release boundaries.
human_authority: Humans approve security requirements, risk, release, exceptions, disclosure, remediation deadlines, and acceptance. Owners must provide qualified review and retain authority to stop, isolate, roll back, or retire the application.
ai_boundary: AI may review authorized code and artifacts, identify patterns, draft tests, and suggest remediation. It must not invent execution evidence, expose secrets, modify production, waive findings, or declare security from static analysis or generated code.
evidence_requirements: Identify artifact, commit, build, environment, tool, rules, coverage, method, result, reviewer, date, and limits. A clean scan or passing test is not proof of absence of vulnerabilities.

why_it_matters: A platform failure or privileged compromise can multiply across workloads. Shared services create concentration risk, hidden authority, cross-tenant leakage, and recovery dependencies that local application controls cannot fully address.
applies_when: Applies to runtime, container, orchestration, developer, CI/CD, data, identity, observability, integration, edge, hosting, and shared service platforms, including managed providers and control planes.

recovery: Freeze or isolate affected zones, revoke credentials, preserve platform and workload evidence, communicate impact, restore from approved known-good state, validate tenant and data boundaries, and reopen when topology, provider, version, threat, or recovery assumptions change.

title: Infrastructure Security
purpose: Protect physical and virtual infrastructure, hosts, storage, operating environments, provisioning paths, administrative planes, and supporting facilities throughout their lifecycle.
why_it_matters: Infrastructure is a common blast-radius boundary. Weak host, image, storage, firmware, or provisioning controls can defeat application security and erase recovery evidence.

required_inputs: Asset inventory, ownership, topology, images, firmware, configurations, identities, access, data, dependencies, patch history, vulnerabilities, telemetry, backup, restore, and facility constraints.
human_authority: Infrastructure owners approve hardening, privileged access, maintenance, exceptions, outage risk, recovery, and retirement; qualified security and operations authorities must review material changes.

title: Hardware Security

A trusted design can be undermined by counterfeit components, altered firmware, open debug ports, insecure manufacturing, untracked substitutions, or physical access that the threat model ignored.

does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only when no hardware asset, physical interface, component trust, supplier, manufacturing, device identity, or lifecycle behavior is affected and an approved exact baseline supports that conclusion.

ai_boundary: AI may analyze authorized bills of materials, schematics, supplier records, configurations, test results, and provenance evidence; identify inconsistencies; and draft controls, inspections, and test plans. human_authority: Owners define identity purpose, resource ownership, access policy, acceptable risk, privileged roles, delegation, review, exceptions, suspension, recovery, and retirement. Humans approve identity proofing, sensitive access, privilege, cross-tenant trust, automated decisions, and disputed or harmful outcomes.

human_authority: Owners approve assurance levels, acceptable authenticators, recovery risk, step-up, provider trust, lockout, support verification, exceptions, and user communication. Humans decide disputed identity, high-impact recovery, emergency access, and residual risk.

title: Cryptography
purpose: Select, apply, verify, and retire cryptographic protections that preserve confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation where required, and controlled recovery for the declared data and trust scope.
why_it_matters: Cryptography can create false confidence when the wrong property, algorithm, mode, key lifecycle, implementation, or trust assumption is used. Strong primitives do not repair poor key management, unauthenticated metadata, weak randomness, unsafe downgrade, or unverified migration.
applies_when: Apply when information, identity, communication, software, hardware, transactions, or evidence requires confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, origin binding, controlled disclosure, or tamper detection.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only when no protected property, cryptographic protocol, key, trust anchor, signature, encrypted data, or migration behavior is affected and an approved exact baseline supports it.
prerequisites: Use data classification, threat model, identity, key, secrets, application, network, hardware, compliance, retention, and recovery baselines. Define security goals, adversary, data states, trust boundaries, interoperability, performance, and recovery authority.
required_inputs: Protection goals, data and protocol inventory, algorithms, modes, parameters, libraries, platforms, randomness, keys, certificates, trust anchors, users, jurisdictions, performance, retention, migration, and acceptance requirements.
human_authority: Owners and qualified security authorities approve cryptographic policy, algorithms, parameters, trust anchors, exceptions, export or regulatory handling, migration, decryption recovery, and retirement. Humans accept residual risk and decide when a protection is no longer adequate.
ai_boundary: AI may inspect authorized cryptographic configurations, dependency versions, protocol traces, certificates, and test evidence; identify known mismatches; draft inventories, tests, and migration options; and explain bounded behavior.
evidence_requirements: Identify asset, protection goal, protocol, algorithm, mode, parameters, implementation, version, key or trust dependency, environment, method, result, owner, and limitation. A successful handshake or encrypted file proves only its declared property and configuration.
failure_anti_patterns: Custom cryptography, obsolete or unapproved primitives, unauthenticated encryption, hard-coded keys, weak randomness, silent downgrade, missing context binding, unverifiable certificates, and treating encryption at rest as complete protection.
recovery: Preserve protected evidence, isolate affected protocols or data, revoke compromised trust, rotate or re-encrypt under approved authority, and use controlled legacy read paths only when risk is accepted. title: Key Management

title: Secrets Management

why_it_matters: Secrets are frequently copied into code, logs, images, tickets, prompts, backups, and developer machines. human_authority: Owners approve secret purpose, storage, access, rotation, emergency retrieval, exceptions, exposure response, and destruction. Humans authorize recovery and decide whether a suspected exposure requires service isolation, user notification, or legal response.
ai_boundary: AI may inspect authorized metadata, configuration references, redacted logs, dependency records, and secret lifecycle evidence; identify likely exposure paths; draft remediation and tests; and explain bounded impact. Preserve forensic records without copying the value, revoke or rotate, isolate consumers, remove replicas, notify owners, and validate replacement. Reassess service continuity, user impact, legal duties, backups, and retention before closure.

title: Threat Modeling

required_inputs: Objective, scope, assets, people, actors, identities, data, flows, interfaces, environments, trust boundaries, assumptions, dependencies, threats, impacts, controls, incidents, evidence, and unresolved questions.
human_authority: Owners identify unacceptable harm, protected populations, risk appetite, legal or safety duties, authority boundaries, and acceptance criteria. ai_boundary: AI may inspect authorized architecture and evidence, enumerate threat hypotheses, compare patterns, draft abuse cases and tests, identify missing assumptions, and challenge the model. It must distinguish source, observation, inference, scenario, likelihood, impact, and recommendation.

title: Vulnerability Management

why_it_matters: A scanner finding may be false, stale, duplicated, unexploitable, or more serious than its score suggests. Untracked assets, unsupported versions, accepted exceptions, and unverified fixes leave the real exposure unknown.

ai_boundary: AI may normalize authorized findings, deduplicate, compare affected versions, enrich with approved intelligence, draft remediation and test plans, and identify missing asset coverage. title: Penetration Testing
purpose: Perform authorized, bounded security testing that validates whether real systems, controls, configurations, interfaces, and recovery paths resist declared attack scenarios.
why_it_matters: A penetration test can reveal control interaction and real exposure that reviews or scanners miss, but an unsafe or poorly scoped test can cause outage, data exposure, legal conflict, or false confidence. A clean result is bounded by scope, time, method, and tester access.
applies_when: Apply when authorized adversarial testing can materially validate security of applications, networks, devices, APIs, identities, cloud resources, facilities, or operational controls.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability when testing would add no material information beyond current verified evidence, the scope is non-consequential and reversible, or authorization and safe test conditions cannot be established. The determination must name the alternative evidence and reopening condition.
prerequisites: Obtain written authorization, target and exclusion list, rules of engagement, contacts, safety and privacy controls, data handling, legal review where needed, rollback and stop conditions, environment access, and incident or support coverage.
required_inputs: Objective, scope, assets, versions, environments, identities, test accounts, allowed methods, exclusions, schedule, rate limits, data constraints, safety limits, threat model, prior findings, evidence, and acceptance criteria.
human_authority: Owners authorize scope, methods, timing, data access, stop conditions, risk, and communication. Test leads protect evidence and people. Humans decide whether testing may affect production, whether a finding requires immediate containment, and whether residual risk is accepted.
ai_boundary: AI may help draft scope, test cases, evidence plans, code or configuration review, and bounded analysis of authorized results. It must preserve authorization and target boundaries, avoid secret exposure, and distinguish observed behavior from inference. It must not initiate testing, expand scope, exploit, persist, exfiltrate, alter, or publish findings without explicit authorized execution and human oversight.
evidence_requirements: Identify authorization, tester or agent, target, version, environment, method, timestamp, account, observed result, evidence location, impact, reproduction boundary, and limitation. Do not retain unnecessary sensitive data or weaponized material.
failure_anti_patterns: Testing without authorization, scope drift, production impact without approval, uncontrolled exploit or data collection, unannounced testing that defeats safety, clean result treated as total security, and findings published without handling controls.
recovery: Stop immediately on unsafe, out-of-scope, or unexpected impact; preserve state and evidence; notify the owner and incident path; clean up or restore under authority; assess data and user impact; and reopen findings or scope when evidence changes.
completion: Authorization, scope, methods, safety, findings, evidence, limitations, remediation, retest, owner decisions, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent review and owner acceptance.

title: Red Teaming
purpose: Conduct authorized, adversary-oriented exercises that test whether people, processes, technology, facilities, and governance detect, resist, contain, communicate, and recover from realistic attack paths.
why_it_matters: Security controls can pass isolated tests while failing as a system. Red teaming exposes assumptions and interactions, but it can also harm people or operations if secrecy, safety, privacy, legal authority, and stop conditions are weak. Exercise success is not proof of total resilience.
applies_when: Apply when an authorized adversary-emulation exercise can reveal material weaknesses in prevention, detection, response, decision-making, physical security, social process, or recovery.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability when the consequence, scope, or authority cannot support a safe exercise and a lower-risk test provides the required evidence, or when no material adversarial path is in scope. Record the alternative and reopening condition.
prerequisites: Require executive or accountable-owner authorization, objective and success criteria, independent exercise control, target and exclusion list, rules of engagement, legal and privacy review, safety contacts, emergency stop, data handling, and defender coordination appropriate to the scenario.
required_inputs: Threat model, intelligence, assets, people, environments, objectives, scenarios, constraints, access, test identities, communications, safety limits, evidence plan, response capability, and acceptance criteria.
human_authority: Owners authorize objectives, scope, acceptable risk, secrecy, safety, communication, and stop conditions. Exercise control can halt activity. Humans decide whether physical, social, production, or high-impact actions are allowed and how affected people are protected.
ai_boundary: AI may help analyze threats, draft scenarios, review authorized exercise evidence, identify control gaps, and propose safe tests. It must preserve authorization, target, identity, time, and handling boundaries. It must not autonomously conduct intrusion, deception, social engineering, persistence, exfiltration, destructive action, or scope expansion without explicit authorization and human supervision.
evidence_requirements: Identify authority, scenario, target, actor, method, time, environment, observation, source, impact, confidence, and limitation. Protect sensitive exercise details and personal information; do not retain operationally dangerous material beyond the approved need.
failure_anti_patterns: Unapproved or indefinite exercise, unclear controller, unsafe secrecy, scope drift, harmful deception, uncontrolled persistence, real data exposure, confusing exercise with incident, and celebrating access without measuring detection or recovery.
recovery: Stop and declare an incident path on unexpected impact, exposure, or scope conflict. Preserve evidence, notify the controller and owner, clean up or restore, protect affected people, assess legal and operational consequences, and revise the model and rules before resuming.
completion: Authority, objective, scenario, scope, safety, evidence, findings, defender behavior, remediation, retest, lessons, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent review and owner acceptance.

title: Digital Forensics

why_it_matters: Digital evidence is volatile, duplicable, privacy-sensitive, and easy to alter. A technically plausible finding is not reliable if the source, acquisition method, time, integrity, analyst, or chain of custody cannot be reconstructed.
applies_when: Apply when system, device, cloud, application, network, identity, log, communication, or data artifacts may support incident response, legal action, safety review, fraud investigation, compliance, or learning.

human_authority: The case owner and qualified forensic lead approve scope, collection, access, privacy handling, analysis, disclosure, retention, and release. Counsel or designated authority controls legal strategy. Humans decide material conclusions and whether evidence may be shared.
ai_boundary: AI may index authorized copies, summarize records, identify patterns, draft timelines, compare artifacts, and propose follow-up questions. It must preserve source identity, integrity, chain of custody, uncertainty, and privacy boundaries. It must not collect, alter, delete, expose, attribute, or declare evidence authentic without authorized human-controlled procedures.
evidence_requirements: Identify source, original state, acquisition method, copy, hash or integrity method, time basis, analyst, tool and version, access, observation, inference, confidence, and limitation. A screenshot, log export, or AI summary is bounded evidence only.

title: Incident Response
purpose: Prepare for, detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover from, communicate, and learn from incidents affecting security, safety, privacy, service, people, property, or trust.
why_it_matters: Incident response is a time-constrained authority problem as well as a technical process. Delayed escalation, unclear ownership, unsafe containment, lost evidence, or premature closure can increase harm and prevent learning.
applies_when: Apply when an actual or suspected event may violate security, privacy, safety, availability, policy, law, contract, user trust, or organizational control.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only for events with no material consequence, no protected asset or person, and a documented routine handling path that preserves evidence and escalation triggers.
prerequisites: Maintain contacts, severity model, authority, playbooks, telemetry, evidence storage, communication paths, legal and privacy guidance, continuity, backup, recovery, and support coverage.
required_inputs: Alert or report, affected assets and people, time, source, scope, severity criteria, evidence, dependencies, responders, authorities, communications, recovery objectives, and known constraints.
human_authority: The incident commander owns coordination and can stop unsafe work. Accountable owners approve containment, service interruption, disclosure, user communication, legal escalation, recovery, and closure. Humans decide material severity, attribution, harm, and residual risk.
ai_boundary: AI may correlate authorized signals, summarize timelines, draft hypotheses, identify affected scope, suggest playbook steps, and track actions. It must label evidence, inference, uncertainty, and recommendation; protect sensitive data; and preserve the incident record. It must not declare an incident, contain, delete evidence, notify external parties, attribute, or close without explicit authority and human control.
evidence_requirements: Identify source, asset, person, event, time basis, method, actor, action, result, confidence, impact, and limitation. Preserve original references and distinguish confirmed, suspected, disproved, and unknown conditions.
failure_anti_patterns: Unowned incidents, severity by volume alone, silent scope changes, destructive containment, lost evidence, premature closure, uncoordinated communication, and postmortems that blame people instead of improving controls.
recovery: Preserve state and evidence, stabilize affected services, protect people, communicate truthfully, and use approved containment, restore, failover, or manual operation. Reassess harm and residual risk after new evidence. Reopen when impact, scope, root cause, or recovery claim changes.
completion: Authority, severity, scope, evidence, actions, communications, recovery, owners, residual risk, lessons, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent review and owner acceptance.

title: Fraud Prevention
purpose: Reduce fraud by identifying deceptive, unauthorized, manipulated, or abusive activity while protecting legitimate users from unjustified suspicion, denial, disclosure, or harm.
why_it_matters: Fraud controls operate under uncertainty and can shift harm onto innocent people. A score, rule, anomaly, or AI prediction is not proof of fraud; opaque or unreviewable action can create financial, access, reputational, and discriminatory harm.
applies_when: Apply when systems detect, prevent, investigate, or respond to fraud involving accounts, payments, identity, transactions, content, suppliers, benefits, or organizational resources.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability when no fraud exposure, transaction, identity, protected outcome, or decision is affected and an approved exact baseline covers the scope. Keep ordinary security and privacy obligations separate.
prerequisites: Use identity, authorization, privacy, security operations, threat, payment, legal, ethics, accessibility, support, and incident baselines. Define harm, protected users, decision owner, review, appeal, and notification authority.
required_inputs: Fraud scenarios, assets, transactions, identities, signals, features, rules, models, thresholds, labels, feedback, data sources, user journeys, false-positive cost, review capacity, appeals, and evidence.
human_authority: Owners approve protected outcomes, signals, thresholds, actions, review, appeal, data use, notification, exceptions, and residual risk. Humans review high-impact denials, account closure, financial holds, vulnerable-user impact, and disputed decisions.
ai_boundary: AI may analyze authorized signals, identify patterns, draft rules or review queues, and recommend investigation. It must expose features, uncertainty, data quality, drift, and limitations; avoid inferring sensitive traits without authority; and preserve an appeal path.
evidence_requirements: Identify subject or transaction, signal, source, feature or rule version, time, decision, reviewer, result, confidence, impact, and limitation. A score or pattern proves neither fraud nor justified action.
failure_anti_patterns: Score as verdict, opaque denial, sensitive-trait proxy, no appeal, feedback loop, unreviewed account closure, target-chasing metrics, and treating customer friction or complaints as fraud evidence.
recovery: Pause or narrow affected controls, preserve evidence, restore legitimate access or funds where appropriate, notify and support affected people, review bias and data quality, and correct downstream records. Reopen on drift, new harm, model or rule change, or disputed outcome.
completion: Scenarios, outcomes, signals, decisions, owners, review, appeal, privacy, evidence, tests, recovery, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent verification and owner acceptance.

title: Abuse Prevention
purpose: Prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to misuse of systems, products, communities, resources, or capabilities while preserving legitimate access, due process, safety, and evidence.
why_it_matters: Abuse is contextual and often targets people with less power. Overbroad controls can silence legitimate use, expose reporters, or punish victims; weak controls can allow harassment, exploitation, fraud, or unsafe behavior to continue.
applies_when: Apply when users, operators, suppliers, agents, or external actors can misuse a product, platform, process, facility, data set, or organizational capability to harm people, property, systems, or trust.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability when no user, public, resource, or trust relationship can be abused within scope and an approved exact baseline documents the conclusion. Do not use absence of reports as proof of absence.
prerequisites: Use trust and safety, privacy, security, fraud, legal, ethics, accessibility, support, incident, and governance baselines. Define prohibited harm, reporting authority, vulnerable populations, response, appeal, and emergency escalation.
required_inputs: Abuse taxonomy, user journeys, reports, signals, content or behavior scope, identity and access, risk, policy, reviewer capacity, victim support, evidence, legal duties, and recovery resources.
human_authority: Owners define protected outcomes, prohibited abuse, enforcement, evidence, reporter protection, appeal, emergency response, and residual risk. Trained humans review high-impact action, vulnerable-person cases, ambiguity, and appeals.
ai_boundary: AI may classify authorized reports, surface patterns, draft queues and safety explanations, and recommend bounded review. It must preserve context, reporter privacy, uncertainty, cultural and accessibility limits, and appeal. It must not label a person an abuser, expose a reporter, remove content, close an account, or make an emergency determination without delegated human authority.
evidence_requirements: Identify report, subject, context, source, time, policy, reviewer, action, confidence, impact, and limitation. Reports and model classifications are allegations or signals until reviewed and bounded.
failure_anti_patterns: Punishing reporters, opaque enforcement, no appeal, context-free classification, proxy discrimination, public accusation, irreversible automation, reviewer burnout, and treating low report volume as low abuse.
recovery: Protect affected people, preserve evidence, pause harmful controls, reverse unjustified actions, provide support and appeal, notify owners, and reassess policy or classifier drift. Reopen on new harm, evasion, policy change, or systematic disparity.
completion: Abuse scope, affected parties, reporting, review, enforcement, appeal, privacy, evidence, recovery, owners, tests, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent verification and owner acceptance.

title: Trust and Safety
purpose: Govern the safety, integrity, fairness, reliability, and human impact of products, services, communities, and automated capabilities that people may rely on or be exposed to.
why_it_matters: Trust is earned through dependable behavior, truthful communication, protection from abuse, and meaningful recourse. Safety can fail through foreseeable misuse, opaque automation, inaccessible controls, weak moderation, or metrics that reward activity while hiding harm.
applies_when: Apply when a product, service, platform, organization, AI capability, or decision process can affect people, public trust, rights, safety, dignity, access, or community conditions.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only when the scope has no affected person, public interaction, consequential decision, abuse path, safety impact, or trust claim and an approved exact baseline documents the determination.
prerequisites: Use user research, risk, privacy, security, abuse, fraud, legal, ethics, accessibility, incident, governance, and operations baselines. Identify vulnerable groups, harm owners, review authority, appeal, and emergency paths.
required_inputs: Users and affected non-users, intended and foreseeable use, harms, policies, reports, incidents, signals, models, controls, support, accessibility, impact measures, evidence, and unresolved concerns.
human_authority: Owners set protected outcomes, unacceptable harm, policy, enforcement, transparency, appeal, emergency response, and risk acceptance. Humans review high-impact decisions, vulnerable-person impact, material policy changes, and claims made to the public.
ai_boundary: AI may summarize authorized reports, identify patterns, draft policy options and tests, and surface uncertainty or conflicting evidence. It must preserve context, privacy, cultural and accessibility boundaries, and human recourse. It must not decide harm, deny rights, remove access, make public claims, or replace accountable review without delegation.
evidence_requirements: Identify claim, affected party, source, context, policy, method, reviewer, result, uncertainty, impact, and limitation. User reports, ratings, model scores, and absence of complaints are bounded signals, not complete safety proof.
failure_anti_patterns: Safety theater, opaque enforcement, no recourse, proxy discrimination, public claims without evidence, optimizing engagement over harm, and treating policy presence as lived safety.
recovery: Protect people, pause harmful behavior, preserve evidence, reverse unjustified action, communicate truthfully, provide support and appeal, and reassess controls and policy. Reopen on new harm, population change, model or policy drift, incident, or credible dissent.
completion: Harms, affected parties, policies, controls, owners, evidence, review, recourse, incidents, recovery, tests, measures, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent verification and owner acceptance.

title: Privacy Engineering
purpose: Translate privacy expectations, obligations, risks, and human control into data, system, process, interface, and lifecycle design.
why_it_matters: Privacy harm can arise even when data is accurate and secure. Excess collection, unexpected reuse, opaque inference, indefinite retention, inaccessible controls, and AI-generated conclusions can remove agency or expose people to decisions they cannot understand or contest.
applies_when: Apply whenever information can identify, describe, infer about, locate, affect, or be linked to a person, household, device, organization, or protected group.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only when no personal, sensitive, linkable, inferred, behavioral, device, or human-impacting information is processed and an approved exact baseline documents the conclusion.
prerequisites: Use data, security, identity, user research, legal, regulatory, ethics, accessibility, records, AI, and operations baselines. Identify data owners, subjects, purposes, jurisdictions, processors, transfers, retention, and rights or support authority.
required_inputs: Data inventory and flows, purpose, classification, source, subjects, consent or legal basis, minimization, inference, sharing, access, retention, deletion, security, user controls, incidents, vendors, and unresolved risks.
human_authority: Privacy and data owners approve purpose, collection, reuse, sharing, retention, deletion, rights handling, automated decisions, exceptions, and residual risk. Humans assess meaningful impact, respond to requests, and decide disputed or high-risk processing.
ai_boundary: AI may inspect authorized schemas and process descriptions, identify data-flow or minimization gaps, draft notices and tests, and summarize privacy evidence. It must not infer consent, legal basis, identity, sensitivity, or acceptable use from data alone. It must not expose personal data, make a rights decision, repurpose data, or deny a request without human authority and review.
evidence_requirements: Identify data, source, subject, purpose, processing, authority, processor, jurisdiction, time, method, result, owner, and limitation. A notice, consent record, deletion log, or privacy scan proves only its declared scope.
failure_anti_patterns: Collect first and define purpose later, consent theater, hidden inference, indefinite retention, deletion that leaves replicas, privacy by policy only, inaccessible rights, and personal data placed into uncontrolled AI context.
recovery: Stop or restrict processing, preserve required evidence, notify owners and affected people as required, correct or delete unauthorized copies, remediate, and reassess harm and legal duties. Reopen on purpose, population, data, processor, jurisdiction, model, or policy change.
completion: Data, purpose, authority, subjects, flows, minimization, rights, retention, deletion, security, sharing, owners, evidence, tests, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending independent verification and owner acceptance.

title: Legal
purpose: Identify, interpret, obtain advice on, and preserve the legal obligations, rights, authorities, liabilities, contracts, disputes, and jurisdictional constraints that affect the work.
why_it_matters: Legal risk is context-specific and can turn on facts, jurisdiction, timing, contract language, or procedural detail. A confident summary, generic compliance statement, or AI-generated interpretation is not a substitute for qualified counsel or accountable decision-making.
applies_when: Apply when law, regulation, contract, rights, litigation, investigation, licensing, intellectual property, employment, safety, privacy, public communication, or jurisdiction affects the scope or consequences.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only when qualified review confirms no legal, contractual, rights, jurisdictional, or dispute effect for the exact scope, version, parties, and time. “Not legal work” is not sufficient.
prerequisites: Identify jurisdictions, entities, parties, activities, data, products, contracts, regulators, counsel, deadlines, records, and decision owners. Preserve legal holds and confidentiality requirements.
required_inputs: Objective, parties, jurisdictions, facts, contracts, policies, data, product or service, claims, notices, deadlines, approvals, prior advice, disputes, source identity, and unresolved legal questions.
human_authority: Qualified counsel or designated legal authority interprets law, privilege, litigation, disclosure, contract, and regulatory strategy. Business owners provide truthful facts, implement approved obligations, and accept non-legal operational tradeoffs only within authority.
ai_boundary: AI may organize authorized legal sources, compare clauses, extract obligations, draft questions and issue registers, and summarize supplied advice with provenance. It must not claim to be counsel, create attorney-client privilege, infer jurisdiction, provide definitive legal advice, conceal adverse facts, or approve a legal position or disclosure.
evidence_requirements: Identify source, jurisdiction, version, party, fact, date, authority, method, reviewer, conclusion or question, and limitation. A legal summary, template, policy, or AI output is not proof of legal sufficiency.
failure_anti_patterns: AI presented as counsel, law copied without jurisdiction, stale advice, hidden facts, privilege in uncontrolled systems, contracts ignored as operational inputs, and compliance asserted from a checklist.
recovery: Pause affected action, preserve records, escalate to counsel, correct the factual record, notify authorized owners, and reassess deadlines and exposure. Reopen on new facts, jurisdiction, contract, law, regulator, dispute, or product change.
completion: Facts, jurisdictions, parties, obligations, sources, counsel status, owners, deadlines, controls, evidence, unresolved questions, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending qualified review and owner acceptance.
source_gaps: Based on the Canonical Section Contract, shared governance, evidence requirements, and the integration roadmap. No jurisdiction, counsel, contract set, regulator, privilege rule, deadline, or legal acceptance authority is assumed by this draft.

title: Regulatory Compliance
purpose: Translate applicable regulatory obligations into owned, testable, evidenced, and continuously reviewed controls without confusing compliance documentation with actual protection or lawful operation.
why_it_matters: Regulation varies by jurisdiction, sector, activity, data, product, and time. A certification, policy, audit, or control description can be stale or incomplete and does not itself prove ongoing compliance.
applies_when: Apply when a regulator, statute, rule, license, order, standard adopted by contract, or public obligation affects the system, organization, product, data, or process.
does_not_apply_when: Record non-applicability only after qualified review of jurisdiction, entity, activity, data, population, product, and time. Preserve the reason, source, reviewer, date, and reopening condition.
prerequisites: Identify legal entities, jurisdictions, regulators, sector, data, contracts, products, controls, counsel, compliance owner, evidence systems, reporting deadlines, and audit or inspection authority.
required_inputs: Regulatory sources, scope, obligations, definitions, controls, policies, procedures, assets, owners, evidence, assessments, incidents, findings, reports, exceptions, and change notices.
human_authority: Compliance and legal owners interpret obligations with qualified counsel, approve applicability, control mapping, reports, exceptions, and regulator communication. Control owners implement and evidence obligations. Humans accept residual risk and attest only to supported facts.
ai_boundary: AI may organize authorized sources, extract obligations, compare control evidence, identify gaps, draft questions, and track changes. It must preserve jurisdiction, source, date, definition, evidence, and uncertainty. It must not declare compliance, provide legal advice, sign an attestation, conceal gaps, or communicate to a regulator without authorized human approval.
evidence_requirements: Identify authority, jurisdiction, source version, obligation, scope, control, environment, method, time, owner, result, and limitation. A policy, certificate, or audit report proves only its stated scope and period.
failure_anti_patterns: Checklist compliance, stale register, unsupported attestation, control description treated as operation, one jurisdiction generalized to another, evidence manufactured for the audit, and exceptions without expiry or owner.
recovery: Mark unsupported claims, preserve evidence, notify compliance and legal owners, remediate or disclose through approved channels, and reassess scope and deadlines. Reopen on regulatory, product, data, entity, jurisdiction, contract, or control change.
completion: Authority, applicability, obligations, controls, owners, evidence, cadence, findings, exceptions, reports, limitations, and reopening conditions are explicit. Status remains CONTENT-COMPLETE pending qualified review and owner acceptance.
